To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the gas-phase chemistry of the uranyl ion depends strongly on the nature of the coordinating anion, and (2) water and alcohol ligands have very different effects on the gas-phase chemistry.
the elimination of HX ligands is the dominant pathway for the gas-phase dissociation of uranyl complexes containing H2O, MeOH, and EtOH ligands.

the gas-phase, water-, and alcohol-coordinated complexes of the general form [UO2(S)n]+ (where S = H2Od, CH3Od or CH3CH20d, d = 1-4) undergo a variety of collision-induced dissociation reactions, including the loss of H2S ligands and HA (where A=Cl, Br or I) and the formation of the bare, hydrated and dehydrated uranyl-anion complex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the gas-phase chemistry of uranyl species.
the production and dissociation reactions of gas-phase, uranyl-containing ions.
the production and collision-induced dissociations of gas-phase uranyl complexes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the gas-phase chemistry of uranyl halide and perchlorate complexes is dominated by ligand elimination reactions, with the exception of the hydrated bromide and perchloride versions, which are the only ones to dissociate to the bare uranyl-anion species.
the gas-phase, hydrated, uranyl cations are stable, with no dissociation of the U-O bonds, but that the alcohol-coordinated versions are more labile and dissociate to produce the uranyl anion.

the dissociation pathways observed for the gas-phase complexes are consistent with the known chemistry of the uranyl ion and its complexes in solution, and that the gas-phase complexes can be considered as reasonable models of the solution species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the dissociation pathways for gas-phase uranyl complexes depend strongly upon the nature of the anionic ligand, and that this is particularly true for H2O-coordinating complexes.

for the halide and perchlorate versions, the gas-phase dissociation reactions are dominated by the intrinsic acidity of the anion, with the uranyl hydroxides being produced as a result of the loss of the anion.
the dissociation of uranyl complexes in the ion trap is governed by the strength of the UO2-S interactions, the strength of UO2-O bonds and the acidity of the S-containing ligands.
The main takeaway from our work is that
gas-phase uranyl complexes containing anions other than OH or ClO4 can be produced and studied using electrospray ionization.
the nature and extent of the ligand coordination sphere, and the identity and number of anionic counterions, can have a profound effect on the CID of uranyl cations.
the uranyl cation is not a particularly stable entity, and the stability of the uranyl cations is strongly affected by the nature of the anions and the ligands.
